text: Bloat shows as left-side distension; tapping the rumen reveals it's full of gas or foam, the animal can't belch out the gas, rumination stops, and the drum-tight rumen presses on the diaphragm, making breathing very hard — temperature stays normal. Causes and responses: a foreign body stuck in the esophagus (corn stalk, fruit, etc.) — a vet should palpate the pharynx/esophagus through the skin to locate the obstruction, try to remove it by hand, and if bloat is severe, pierce the rumen with a trocar to release gas, always followed by antibiotic to prevent peritonitis. Wet young grass — can strike suddenly, especially grazing wet pasture in the morning or overeating young grass at the start of the rainy season, and can cause sudden death; prevention is not turning a hungry animal loose on risky grazing; treatment is 300–500 ml of oil given orally. Urea poisoning — from licking leftover urea in a bag, or from an improperly gradual urea-spraying technique on straw feed: severe bloat, muscle tremors progressing to incoordination, death within 2 hours; treatment is 2–5 liters of vinegar given orally.
caveat: See also the separate entries on trocar use for severe bloat and on urea/pesticide poisoning first response for related detail.
